findings.statement: The AI system used to produce loan-approval recommendations falls within the high-risk category under Article 6(2): it is an AI system used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons, listed in Annex III point 5(b), and the company uses it for all consumer loan applications in the EU.

Because the company uses the AI system under its authority for its business, it acts as the system's deployer within Article 3(4) and must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying it.

The company must assign the human oversight of the system to employees with the necessary competence, training and authority, and the oversight must enable those employees to understand the system's capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the recommendation and disregard, override or reverse it.

To the extent the company exercises control over the input data, it must ensure that the income, employment-history, debt and other financial data fed to the system are relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the system's intended purpose.
The company must keep the logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent they are under its control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and of at least six months.

Before using the system at the workplace the company must inform workers' representatives and the affected employees that they will be subject to its use, and it must inform applicants that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system because the system assists in making decisions relating to natural persons.

Applicants subject to a loan decision taken by the company on the basis of the system's output, which produces legal effects on them, have the right to obtain from the company clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

Prior to the first use of the system the company must perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights, covering its processes, the categories of affected persons, the specific risks of harm, the human-oversight implementation and complaint mechanisms, because it is a deployer of a creditworthiness-evaluation system listed in Annex III point 5(b).
The company must take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among its staff who operate the system and review its recommendations.

The processing of applicants' income, employment history, existing debts and other financial information is processing of personal data that is lawful only under at least one of the exhaustive bases in Article 6(1), such as necessity for the performance of the loan contract under point (b) or legitimate interests under point (f), and the company must secure such a basis for the processing.

The processing must comply with the data protection principles in Article 5(1), including lawfulness, fairness and transparency and data minimisation, which constrain how much and how applicants' financial data may be collected and used in the AI-based assessment.

The system's analysis of applicants' financial data constitutes profiling under Article 4(4) as automated processing evaluating their economic situation, and the loan decision produces legal effects concerning applicants; because employees make the final decision after reviewing the recommendation, the decision is not one based solely on automated processing within the meaning of Article 22(1).

The company must carry out a data protection impact assessment prior to the processing, because the AI-based credit assessment is a systematic and extensive evaluation of applicants' personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, on which decisions producing legal effects (loan approval or refusal) are based.

If the company qualifies as a financial entity listed in DORA Article 2(1), for example a credit institution, payment institution or crowdfunding service provider, it must have a sound ICT risk management framework covering the AI credit-assessment system and use and maintain updated ICT systems, protocols and tools that are reliable and technologically resilient.

summaries.relevance: Establishes the high-risk status that triggers the whole AI Act layer of the answer: the deployer duties, the fundamental rights impact assessment and the explanation right all attach only because the system is high-risk.

Names the company's exact use case, AI evaluation of the creditworthiness of natural persons for loan decisions, as a high-risk area, anchoring the classification and the special deployer duty attached to creditworthiness deployers.
Fixes the company's role as deployer because it uses the system under its authority in its business, identifying which set of AI Act obligations governs the scenario.
Obliges the deployer to run the loan-assessment system in line with the provider's instructions for use, the baseline operating constraint on the scenario's use case.
Directly governs the scenario's employee review step by requiring that the persons assigned to human oversight have the competence, training and authority to perform it.

Defines what the oversight over the loan recommendations must enable, including automation-bias awareness and the ability to disregard, override or reverse the output, shaping how the human review must work.
Adds the input-data quality duty covering the financial data fed to the system, conditioned on the deployer's control over that data.
Imposes the minimum six-month retention of the system's automatically generated logs, a concrete record-keeping consequence of using this high-risk system in production.
Requires informing the employees who review the recommendations about their exposure to the high-risk system before it is used at the workplace.
Requires informing the applicants themselves that they are subject to the system's use in decisions relating to them.

Gives loan applicants a directly enforceable right to clear and meaningful explanations of the AI's role and the main elements of the decision, the AI Act's principal transparency response in this scenario.
Makes a fundamental rights impact assessment mandatory before first use and expressly covers deployers of creditworthiness-evaluation systems, a duty that runs alongside the GDPR impact assessment.
Imposes on the company, as deployer, the duty to ensure AI literacy among staff operating and reviewing the system.
Answers the question's core lawfulness concern: processing applicants' financial data for the AI assessment is lawful only under one of the exhaustive Article 6(1) bases.
Frames the binding principles of lawful, fair and transparent processing and data minimisation that limit how applicants' financial data may be collected and used.
Supplies the profiling definition under which the system's automated evaluation of applicants' economic situation falls.
Delimits the solely automated decision regime and, read with the scenario's employee review, places the loan decision outside the most restrictive automated-decision rule.
Captures AI-based credit scoring as a systematic and extensive automated evaluation on which legal-effect decisions rest, mandating an impact assessment.
Sets the controller's duty to carry out that impact assessment before the processing begins.
Determines whether DORA reaches the company at all, since its duties attach only to the financial entities the article lists.
Obliges qualifying entities to maintain a sound ICT risk management framework that must cover the AI credit-assessment system.
Requires the ICT systems and tools supporting loan decisions to be reliable, appropriately sized and technologically resilient.

actions: Settle whether the company qualifies as a financial entity listed in DORA Article 2(1), for example as a credit institution, payment institution or crowdfunding service provider, since DORA's ICT risk duties attach only to such entities.

Determine whether the company is also the system's provider, for instance if it developed the system in-house, markets it under its own name or substantially modifies it (AI Act Articles 3(3) and 25(1)), which would engage provider obligations under Article 16 and the conformity assessment under Article 43.

Settle the GDPR lawful basis under Article 6(1) relied on for processing applicants' income, employment, debt and other financial data for the AI assessment, including the supporting necessity or balancing analysis.

Verify the extent to which the company exercises control over the input data fed to the system, which conditions the scope of its AI Act Article 26(4) duty on input-data relevance and representativeness.
Confirm whether the AI system is obtained from an ICT third-party service provider, which would bring DORA Article 28 third-party risk-management and contractual requirements into play.
